title: Hierarchical Architecture and Its Failure Mode

questions.question: A task has departments with separate responsibilities, and each department can break its work into smaller jobs. What architecture mirrors that structure?
options: A hierarchy with managers, sub-managers, and worker leaves
A flat list where every agent receives every task
A round-robin chat where roles change each turn
A single worker with no decomposition or delegation
questions.explanation: Nested managers mirror departments that can decompose work into their own sub-jobs, with worker leaves doing the final tasks. A flat list sends work to peers but does not represent that real responsibility structure.

questions.question: When does the lesson recommend a sequential pipeline instead of a hierarchy?
options: When departments have truly independent sub-teams
When every leaf has a distinct and necessary role
When sub-managers can summarize their own outputs
When the task is one linear flow pretending to be a tree
questions.explanation: A tree adds value when real independent sub-teams can work under sub-managers. If the job is one linear sequence with dependencies, manager layers add routing and summaries without exposing independent branches.

questions.question: The top manager sends a legal review task to a finance sub-manager. What is the likely failure path?
options: The legal result is verified because the branch name is similar
The top manager is forced to stop before collecting any output
Finance does its assigned work, leaving the legal question unanswered
The finance worker rewrites the original user request automatically
questions.explanation: The finance branch can faithfully complete the task it received while leaving the legal question unanswered; the failure begins in top-level decomposition. A similar branch name does not validate that the sub-manager owns the requested domain.

questions.question: Two sub-managers disagree and the top manager repeatedly re-delegates work. Which control limits this loop?
options: An explicit reconciliation-round or step budget
A rule that every worker must accept the first answer
A deeper tree with additional manager layers
A longer shared transcript for all workers
questions.explanation: A reconciliation-round or step budget limits how often managers can reassign disputed work, so disagreement eventually exits to a decision or escalation. Adding tree depth creates more delegation points and can extend the loop.

questions.question: A top-level summary states that a claim is false, while the sub-manager only said it could not be verified. What safeguard helps catch this meaning drift?
options: Let the same top manager review its own conclusion
Attach provenance from each synthesis back to leaf outputs
Increase the manager's confidence in the summary
Remove the uncertain wording before storing the output
questions.explanation: Provenance links each summary claim back to the leaf output that supports it, allowing a reviewer to see where “could not verify” became “false.” Asking the same manager to check its own conclusion does not restore the lost evidence.

questions.question: A project has only a few clear steps and no true departments. Which design choice best follows the lesson?
options: Create a finance branch to test a second manager
Use a sequential or flat supervisor pattern instead of nested managers
Let all managers debate freely until they reach agreement naturally
Add more hierarchy levels to improve observability
questions.explanation: A few clear sequential steps fit a pipeline or flat supervisor: each stage passes its result to the next without inventing departments. More levels increase coordination work without adding genuine parallel branches.
